schools.summary: Gill glosses the voice as heard in the law and by the prophets. Calvin reads the promise of pre-eminence as bounty rather than title, the diversity of expression and the repetition alike tending to confirmation; and what he draws from the catalogue that follows is not its grandeur but its length, since the enumeration shows to how many necessities we are exposed, so that if we are blessed in city and field we can no more move a foot than stand still except by God's blessing.

Henry reads the order itself as doctrine: the blessings are put before the curses to intimate that God is slow to anger but swift to show mercy, and that it is his delight to bless; it is better to be allured to good by a filial hope of God's favour than frightened to it by a servile fear of his wrath. He sets the conditions out in three — diligent hearkening, doing and keeping all the commandments to the end, and turning aside neither to superstition nor to profaneness, and above all not after other gods. On the word overtake he notes that good people, sensible of their unworthiness, are sometimes ready to fly from the blessing, but it shall find them out and follow them notwithstanding.

Clarke opens with the argument of the whole chapter: the blessings on the obedient, the privileges of the faithful, the curses on the idolatrous, and the long account of the miseries, ending with the scattering among all nations.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as a heading rather than a promise, the thought that closed the previous discourse forming the theme of the description that follows, with obedience as the indispensable condition — repeated at the commencement, in the middle, and at the close. Ellicott takes the promise literally and finds a divine name in it, the Lord making Israel Most High, and gathers the parallels where a name of God is laid on a people or a place.

themes: blessings set before curses
the Lord will make thee Most High
the conditions stated three ways
how many necessities the list implies

schools.summary: Gill has the blessings come from heaven by the direction of providence, freely and beyond their expectations and deserts; he fills in the city with spacious houses, walled and populous towns, health and plenty and prospering merchandise, as Aben Ezra notes, and promises children many and living, adding Grotius' opinion that the promise was eminently fulfilled in Mary.

Clarke hangs four observations on the image of a journey — the voice of God must be heard, since without revelation the divine will cannot be known; when God speaks men must hearken, for he who does not hearken will not obey; he who hearkens must set out for the kingdom; and those who run in the way of God's testimonies receive the promises in the time and place where each is most needed. He divides city and field by occupation, and extends the last clause to every animal employed in domestic and agricultural use. Wesley makes the blessing a reversal of the world's usual chase, since what others follow and never overtake shall follow after Israel and be thrown into its lap.

Ellicott calls overtake a beautiful expression, meaning that the blessing comes home when least expected, and cites the prophet's question whether God's words did not overtake the fathers; the same, he notes, is true of the curses. Keil and Delitzsch read the structure instead, marking that the following verses describe the blessing's effect on every situation the nation might be in — its enemies, its trade, and its standing among the nations.

themes: blessings that overtake rather than are chased
the city and the field
the fruit of the body
each promise in its own season

schools.summary: Gill notes the Targums restrain the basket to the firstfruits and the cake of the first dough, but takes it himself for every vessel holding provisions for present use, which should never be empty; and he reads the going out and coming in of all business and employments, in every office public or private, and particularly in going out to war and returning.

Clarke glosses the basket as the olive gathering and vintage and the store as the kneading-trough or remainder, then passes on Harmer's proposal at length: that the two words mean the travelling basket and the leathern bag, since one occurs elsewhere only of the conveyance for the firstfruits and the other only of the utensils used in the hurried journey out of Egypt. Hasselquist reports such palm-leaf bags still used in Turkey, and as figs and raisins are carried in a goat's skin in Barbary, so merchandise might have been; understood so, the verse promises success in commerce. Wesley reads the store simply as a storehouse always well replenished.

Ellicott sets out how far the versions part, since the word for store is identical in form with the word for kneading troughs, and all the Targums and Jewish commentators take the contrast that way — firstfruits against prepared dough, the corn-vessel against the meal-vessel, or, as Rashi has it, the vessel for things moist against the vessel for things dry. He prefers the Septuagint's simpler reading, the portion brought out now against what is put away for later. On the going out and coming in he sees a further meaning in the entrance and departure of Christ, and quotes Rashi that a man's departure from the world should be sinless as his entrance.

debates: What the basket and store are. Clarke follows Harmer in making them travelling vessels and reading the verse of commerce; Ellicott prefers the Septuagint's present portion against future store, against all the Targums and Jewish commentators, who divide them by the state of the food.
themes: what the basket and the store were
Harmer's travelling basket
going out and coming in
success in commerce

7.pericope_label: The enemies routed and the storehouses blessed

schools.summary: Gill names the nations it happened to — Philistines, Moabites, Syrians, Edomites and Ammonites, especially in the days of David — and takes the storehouses for barns, granaries and cellar, the benefit being preservative: the grain kept from vermin, the casks from bursting.

Clarke reads the verse as security against foreign invasion or the total discomfiture of invaders, who come one way in the firmest and most united manner and flee seven ways utterly broken; and on the commanded blessing he gets a doctrine, that everything a man has comes by divine appointment and nothing casually.

Ellicott quotes Rashi for the manner of the flight, that the terrified scatter in every direction, and points to the Midianites before Gideon and the Syrians abandoning their camp. On the storehouses he finds the antithesis the English hides — the gathering in against the putting forth of the hand, revenue and expenditure alike prospered — and reads the closing promise as fixity of tenure in the divine inheritance. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as a wish rather than a prediction, that the Lord may put the blessing at Israel's disposal in its granaries and in all its business.

themes: flee seven ways
income and expenditure alike blessed
nothing received casually
fixity of tenure in the inheritance

schools.summary: Gill takes establish of continuance and settlement — God keeping them separated for his service, settling them in the land and confirming their privileges natural, civil and religious — and notes the Targum of Jonathan's reading that the Word of the Lord shall establish thee. Calvin will not let the earthly reading stand alone: the promise refers to earthly blessings, yet rises higher, so that the Israelites, led on by degrees, should embrace God alone according to the covenant with Abraham, being assured they would be blessed in death as well as life; their adoption was gratuitous, yet since they were called unto purity their sanctification should be firm and perpetual if they walked in his commandments.

Clarke reduces the verse to one sentence and one warning: this is the sum of all blessings, to be made holy and preserved in holiness, and here is the solemn condition, that if they did not keep God's testimonies as the regulators of their lives the curses and not the blessings must be their portion. Wesley says the same more shortly, that God would confirm the covenant by which he had separated them as a holy and peculiar people.

Ellicott traces the Hebrew and finds the promise means either to maintain them in that position or to raise them into it, the word having branched into two lines of thought — permanence and perpetuity in Jewish literature, and, through the Septuagint, the New Testament word for resurrection. Keil and Delitzsch look backwards for the oath, which rested on the promises given to the patriarchs and was contained implicitly in them; the name of the Lord is the revelation of his glorious nature, and is named upon Israel when Israel is transformed into the glory of that nature.

themes: establish, maintain, or raise up
a word that gave the New Testament resurrection
the name of the Lord named upon Israel
earthly blessing that rises higher

schools.summary: Gill lists what the nations would see them called — his children, his people, his portion and his inheritance — and how the fact would be evident, from the care he took, the provision he made and the protection they had; on the plenty he promises an affluence of all temporal good things, again reporting the Targum of Jonathan's Word of the Lord for the divine name.

Wesley makes it their being in truth God's people and children, a most excellent and glorious people under the peculiar care and countenance of the great God; and of the repeated promises he observes that the doubling of the words is itself part of the gift.

Ellicott gives the literal Hebrew, that the name of Jehovah has been called upon thee — a passive construction where ours is active — and matches the neighbours' dread with the prophet's word that they shall fear and tremble for all the goodness God procures for Jerusalem, so that what they feel is awe rather than hostility. Keil and Delitzsch look past this to the figure the passage drives at, that by such blessings the Lord would make Israel the head and not the tail, an image taken from life whose sense is given literally in the clause that follows.

themes: called by the name of the Lord
awe rather than hostility
the head and not the tail
repetition as part of the promise

schools.summary: Gill observes that the Lord has treasures of snow and hail and wind, but that his good treasure here is rain. Calvin reads the rain as an argument about dependence — we attain nothing by industry except so far as God vouchsafes good success, all our efforts without his secret blessing being useless fatigue, though God does not mean us to sit idle. He then raises the difficulty the chapter invites, why so many despisers of God prosper, and answers that God diffuses his bounty promiscuously over the whole race, doing good to the ungodly because he is their Creator and hiding his judgment as in the darkness of night; yet to them not a drop of true goodness is dispensed, since unless a sense of his paternal favour is awakened the blessing ceases to exist, and they are fed unto the day of slaughter, while what God promises his own he seasons with spiritual salt.

Clarke names the clouds, so that fructifying showers descend at all requisite times and the vegetative principle in the earth exerts itself; Wesley calls the treasure the heaven or air, God's storehouse, where he lays up rain or wind for use.

Ellicott brings a Jewish saying to the verse: there are three keys in the hand of the Holy One which he has not entrusted to a messenger — of the rains, of birth, and of the resurrection of the dead — and the proof text cited for the first is this very verse.

outliers: Calvin's extended theodicy on the prosperity of the wicked, which turns a verse about rain into an argument about how God's bounty can fall on men to whom no blessing is truly dispensed.
themes: the good treasure is rain
the three keys not given to a messenger
why the ungodly prosper
blessings seasoned with spiritual salt

13.pericope_label: The head and not the tail

schools.summary: Gill takes the promise for dominion rather than subjection, the head signifying rulers and governors and the tail the common people, or the one honourable and the other mean and base, and again notes the Targum's Word of the Lord; on going aside he glosses departing from the words as a rule and turning out of them as a path.

Clarke makes the figure do the work: the way of obedience is a straight way and goes right forward, and he who declines to right or left goes astray and misses heaven. Wesley qualifies the promise — chief of all people in power, or at least in dignity and privileges, so that even those not under their authority should reverence them; it was so in David's and Solomon's time, and would have been so much oftener had they performed the conditions.

Ellicott raises the syntax: the sentence may attach to the condition before it, but the Septuagint and apparently the Targums begin a fresh sentence here, and he thinks the second construction carries a thought quite at home in Jewish literature, that obedience begets obedience. Keil and Delitzsch look forward instead and describe the shape of the curse to come, proclaimed in a sixfold repetition of the word cursed and then unfolded in ever increasing extent and fearfulness.

themes: rulers and subjects, not head and tail
a straight way that goes right forward
obedience begetting obedience
the shape of the curse to come

schools.summary: Gill points back only to the hearkening the chapter has urged. Calvin asks why the catalogue should be so long and answers from the temper of the hearers: this list is longer than the one proclaimed from Sinai because the Spirit of God foresaw that the sluggishness of the people needed sharper stimulants, so that they might not only fear but be roused by constant reminding. He notes the shape of the sixfold sentence — city and field, seed and meal, and three kinds of fruit.

Henry puts it as a turning of the cloud, and argues the equity of the sentence, since this is no curse causeless. Three things bring it: despising God, which bespeaks the highest contempt imaginable; disobeying him, since none fall under the curse but those who rebel; and deserting him, for God never casts us off till we first cast him off. He traces the extent along the three lines the blessing had run — wherever the sinner goes, whatever he has, whatever he does — and finds the whole the reverse of the blessing above, as whatever bliss there is in heaven there is in hell not only the want of it but the contrary to it.

Wesley says of the word overtake what Henry says in nearly the same words: the sinner shall not escape, though he vainly hope to, for there is no running from God but by running to him, no flying from his justice but by flying to his mercy.
Ellicott marks the hinge in a sentence, that the verses from here to the end of the forty-eighth are the contrast to the first fourteen.

themes: the dark side of the cloud
despising, disobeying, deserting
no running from God but to him
why the list of curses is the longer

schools.summary: Gill will not gloss these verses at all, referring the reader back to the corresponding promises, since the curses are delivered out in form as the reverse of the blessings and the one is directly opposite to the other. Calvin takes the going out and coming in as a merism for the whole course of life, so that ill success is pronounced on every undertaking; on the three Hebrew words he leaves the philology open, since however they are parsed the sum is that God would be against them, from which he draws the lesson that all men's endeavours are useless unless they seek success from him. Gill reports Jarchi's reading of the first word as penury, with their very blessings turned into curses.

Clarke divides the three by their effects — cursing their state, vexation the grief and anguish of heart, rebuke the continual marks of God's displeasure. Wesley locates vexation in the mind, arising from disappointed hopes and the presages of approaching misery, and takes rebuke to come not so much in words as by cross providences and sharp afflictions.

Keil and Delitzsch make the correspondence exact, these four verses answering precisely to the four that pronounced the blessing, and notice the one departure from the order, that basket and kneading-trough are named before the fruit of the body; the three words for the curse they take as synonyms strung together to strengthen the thought. Ellicott notices what our version hides, that all three nouns carry the definite article, as though they were so many named diseases, and reads the following clause as the exact reverse of the blessing on the storehouses; on the last words he observes that Moses and Jehovah are here identified, where the prophets say thus saith the Lord.

themes: the blessing turned over
the curse, the terror, the rebuke
a merism for the whole of life
Moses speaking in God’s own name

schools.summary: Gill notes the pestilence is not merely to come but to continue, and takes the consumption for an emaciation through famine or wasting disease till men are skin and bones. Calvin generalises: diseases are the lictors of God and finally his executioners, so that he does not merely send the pestilence but causes it to cleave, glued upon them till it consume them in the Holy Land itself; the multitude of diseases are all so many ministers prepared to execute his vengeance, and though they are contracted in various ways, especially by intemperance, this does not prevent God from smiting transgressors with them where no natural cause appears. Of the two blights he says one is an emptying of the ears by a dry east wind and the other the sudden heat of the sun on corn moistened with dew — and though these arise from natural causes, God so controls the atmosphere that its unwholesomeness is his undoubted scourge.

Clarke renders the verb that the Lord shall cement the plague to them, the Greek having it that he will glue and inseparably attach the death; and he takes the catalogue word by word out of the Hebrew — atrophy through lack of food, a burning inflammatory fever, a rapidly consuming cancer, and burning upon burning, which he refers also to the agony of a mind abandoned by God. The sword is war, enemies without and civil broils within; and of the seven plagues he counts five falling on their bodies and two on their substance.

Ellicott notes the pestilence as one of the four sore judgments threatened against Jerusalem and marks the range of what follows, a gradual consumption of Israel in the land of promise before any actual captivity; he confirms the rarity of the words, two occurring only here and in the parallel curse in Leviticus and two nowhere else, and glosses each from Rashi. Keil and Delitzsch add the drought that goes with them, a heaven of brass and an earth of iron, with dust and ashes falling instead of rain, explained from a country where in great heat the wind takes the form of a burning sirocco.

themes: a plague glued to them
diseases as the lictors of God
four words found almost nowhere else
the burning sirocco

23.pericope_label: A heaven of brass and an earth of iron

schools.summary: Gill says the heaven is like brass not for clearness or splendour but for dryness and hardness, no moisture in it or passing through it, and explains the showers of dust from soil parched and crumbled, raised by the wind and let down again, as the Targum of Jonathan also has it. Calvin sets the threat against the promises it reverses, since God often promises the rain of autumn and of spring by the prophets and in many places threatens to withhold them; whence we gather that not a drop falls except as God distils it, the more so because Canaan was not watered like Egypt by the industry of man but by the bounty of heaven. He notes that the words specify the heaven over our head and the earth under our feet, God's weapons being prepared above and below.

Clarke puts it in terms of an atmosphere unreplenished with vapours, so that the ground lies wholly intractable, and draws the point of the image — that God shows himself Lord of nature, and that drought and sterility are not casualties but proceed from his immediate appointment. He confirms the showers of dust from travellers: whole caravans buried under sand, and Thevenot's report that such showers fill the eyes and ears and nostrils of all they fall on.

Ellicott adds a second turn of the screw, that the metals stand not only for the drought but for God's refusal to remove it, pointing to Jeremiah's intercession answered by the order not to pray for this people for their good. Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the defeat that follows, the exact opposite of the earlier promise, where Israel becomes what one Hebrew word calls a moving to and fro, a ball for all the kingdoms of the earth to play with.

themes: brass and iron for hardness, not shine
drought as appointment, not accident
grief permitted and relief withheld
a ball for the kingdoms to play with

25.pericope_label: Defeat, dispersion, and the unburied dead

schools.summary: Gill dates the defeat rather than describing it, instancing the Philistines and afterwards the Assyrians, Babylonians and Romans, and counts it a very grievous calamity to have no other burial than in the bowels of beasts and birds, citing a Jewish record of a persecution in Spain. Calvin reads the verse for what it says about courage — the going out one way and returning seven showing that the bravery of men is in God's power, so that he can make cowards of the boldest whenever he pleases, which is why he calls himself the God of hosts. Of the unburied carcass he explains why the want of a grave counts as a curse at all: it is a sign of God's paternal favour that we should be distinguished from the brutes, the rites of burial rousing us to the hope of resurrection; yet he cautions that such punishments are common to the pious and the reprobate, since the rich man was honourably buried while the bodies of the pious have been cast out.

Ellicott marks the defeat as the contrary of the earlier promise and takes up the word removed, which is literally a removing, the Greek here having the very word used in the New Testament for the dispersion. On the clause that none should fray them away he recalls Rizpah, who watched her children's bodies for half a year and suffered neither the birds by day nor the beasts by night — here, he says, there shall be no one to do it. Keil and Delitzsch pass on to the four incurable diseases that follow, identifying the ulcer of Egypt with elephantiasis and the tumour with the disease the Philistines were smitten with.

themes: one way out and seven ways back
the God of hosts and the courage of men
burial as a mark of paternal favour
no Rizpah to fray them away

schools.summary: Gill reports that some understand the botch of the leprosy called elephantiasis, frequent among the Egyptians, and passes on two travellers' accounts of what the Nile does to the skin, though others take it for the boils and blains of the Egyptian plague. Calvin reads the clause historically: whether the plagues meant are the extraordinary ones of the deliverance or the ordinary diseases prevalent in Egypt before — and he thinks the latter more probable — Moses signifies that while the Egyptians were smitten God's people escaped, a distinction that could not have happened naturally, so that the threat is that God will deal with them as they had seen him deal with the heathen.

Clarke identifies it outright with elephantiasis and describes it at length as the most horrid disease that can afflict human nature, referring the reader to Aretaeus and quoting Lucretius that it is bred about the streams of the Nile and nowhere else. He derives the emerods from a root meaning to be raised up, finds the scab has no Hebrew verb behind it but an Arabic word for a distemper of the eye, and makes the itch a burning one, commonly called St Anthony's fire; being inflicted by God's justice, he says, they could not be cured by human art. Wesley reads the botch as the boils and blains, spreading from head to foot.

Ellicott notes the word is the same as the boil of the Egyptian plague and quotes Rashi that it was moist inside and dry outside, adding that a learned Dalmatian Jew of his acquaintance had seen many such cases among the Hungarian and Polish Jews. He glosses the other three from Rashi and the Levitical law, and is exact about the incurability: not that the diseases are in themselves incurable, but that they should have them incurably.

debates: Whether the botch is the leprosy or the plague-boil. Clarke and Gill's first sense make it elephantiasis, the disease peculiar to Egypt; Wesley and Ellicott identify it with the boils and blains inflicted on the Egyptians at the exodus, the same Hebrew word being used there.
themes: what the botch of Egypt was
Aretaeus and Lucretius on elephantiasis
incurable, or had incurably
Israel spared what Egypt suffered

schools.summary: Gill traces the madness to its occasion, the calamities that had befallen them and the force of the diseases upon them. Calvin thinks this the heaviest stroke in the list though the least felt: the prophets often speak of God smiting the wicked with a spirit of giddiness, and from that blindness it comes that men rush wilfully into vile lusts, shudder at no crime and throw away the remedies in their hands. The common apprehension of men is not much disturbed by this form of vengeance, and yet it is far more severe than any bodily disease; the poets imagined the wicked agitated by the furies because experience taught them that men became so senseless only by a secret impulse from God.

Clarke agrees the blindness is both physical and mental, the scab destroying their eyes and the judgments of God confounding their understandings, and gives the astonishment as stupidity and amazement, adding the old saying that those whom God is determined to destroy he first infatuates — which he applies, with some feeling, to the powers of Europe in his own day. Wesley reads blindness of mind, so that they should not know what to do, and astonishment as wonder and horror at the strangeness of their calamities.

Keil and Delitzsch count three maladies of the mind and argue that the middle one is mental rather than bodily, since its position between idiocy and confusion of the understanding points that way, as does the next verse, where Israel gropes at noonday like a blind man in the dark. Ellicott only notes that all three words occur together in Zechariah, where the threat seems aimed at the enemies of Jerusalem rather than at Jerusalem itself.

outliers: Clarke's application of the proverb about infatuation before ruin to the European powers of his own day, in a note otherwise about Hebrew disease-names.
themes: madness, blindness, astonishment
a stroke felt least and worst
whom God would destroy he first infatuates
the furies as a heathen guess at providence

29.pericope_label: Groping at noonday, and the spoiling

schools.summary: Gill argues from the comparison itself that the blindness must be of the mind, since to the blind darkness and light are alike and the force of at noonday is that they cannot judge of things as clear as noon. Calvin reads the plundering in an order of increasing pain, the most painful put first — not the wife torn from her husband's bosom but the betrothed virgin defiled — then houses and vineyards, then flocks and herds, then the children taken in their parents' sight, so that their eyes fail with grief and their hands, as if dead, cannot help them; and he gives two reasons why the robbers should be strangers, that less consideration is to be expected from barbarians, and that Israel might not suppose it had only neighbouring nations to deal with.

Clarke turns the verse on the history, that perhaps no people have been more oppressed and spoiled, and that they still grope at noonday, not discovering that the rejection of their own Messiah is the cause of their calamities; and he will not pass the catalogue without a word to his own readers, that though they have grievously sinned they have grievously suffered, and Christians should not by unkind treatment increase their miseries. Wesley puts it in a line, that in the clearest matters they should grossly mistake.

Ellicott sets the clause against the promise to Joshua that he should prosper if he followed the book of the law, and against Isaiah's sentence that the wisdom of their wise men shall perish. Keil and Delitzsch gloss not prospering as not hitting upon the road that led to the goal, and add one exact note of Ellicott's on the phrase rendered none to rescue: the Hebrew is literally thou shalt have no saviour, which the times before the judges — themselves called saviours — must often have fulfilled.

themes: blindness of mind, not of the eye
the order of the plundering
thou shalt have no saviour
a warning to Clarke’s own readers

32.pericope_label: Children taken, labour eaten, reason lost

schools.summary: Gill observes that this was not true of the Babylonish captivity, where sons and daughters went with their parents and returned with them, but has been verified often since the Roman captivity, children taken by force to be brought up in another religion by edicts of kings and popes; and of the madness at the end he makes it the sum of everything threatened, giving two instances from Germany where whole communities destroyed themselves and their families.

Clarke says the same of Spain and Portugal, where Jewish children were taken by order of government and educated in the Popish faith, noting instances even in Protestant countries. Wesley reads the verse more plainly — children given or sold by their conquerors, eyes consumed partly with grief and partly with vain expectation of their return, a hand with no power to rescue and no money to ransom — and describes the madness from within, men put out of the possession of their own souls and abandoned to despair, with the moral that those who walk by sight and not by faith are in danger of losing reason itself.

Ellicott calls this perhaps the most pathetic piece of description in the whole chapter, since the bordering nations were accustomed to carry off not only cattle but children for slaves, and sets Jeremiah's Rachel weeping in Ramah beside it — with the difference that it would not always be added, as it was there, that they shall come again from the land of the enemy. The last clause he thinks very remarkable in the Hebrew, meaning literally that thou shalt have no hand toward God, and compares Moses in the fight with Amalek: here the eyes fail with looking, but cannot look up.

themes: a captivity that kept the children
no hand toward God
Rachel weeping in Ramah
mad for the sight of the eyes

35.pericope_label: The botch in the knees, and the king in captivity

schools.summary: Gill notes only that a sore in those parts is very painful and not easily cured. Calvin sets it in a wider frame: since death is common to the race all must be subject to sickness, but because offences are not all alike God keeps a just proportion in his punishments, and what is spoken of here is not common maladies but the incurable ones by which he openly shows his vengeance. Of the king's captivity he says it is the prophecy they found least credible, since all their safety depended on their kingly government, and quotes Jeremiah magnifying that evil above the rest — the breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord, taken in their pits. On serving wood and stone he finds an antithesis implied: because they refused to submit to the true God, they should become the slaves of idols.

Clarke and Wesley keep it short — Clarke identifying the sore with the boil already named, Wesley observing that the calamity is universal, since even the king cannot avoid it, and irrecoverable, since he who should rescue them is lost with them, and that what was formerly their choice and delight now becomes their plague.

Keil and Delitzsch call the sore joint-leprosy but will not let the clause from sole to crown be restricted to it, since in that form the upper parts often remain normal; they add what mattered most, that leprosy excluded a man from fellowship with the Lord and deprived the nation of its character as a nation of God, which is what connects this verse to the captivity following. Ellicott counts the kings who went into captivity — Jehoahaz to Egypt, Jeconiah and Zedekiah to Babylon, Hoshea apparently with Samaria — and argues from a silence that no later writer could have concealed the existence of two kingdoms or avoided all allusion to the throne of David.

themes: joint-leprosy and the whole body
the anointed taken in their pits
slaves to the idols they chose
an argument from what Moses does not know

schools.summary: Gill puts it in terms of the neighbours, who should hear of their overthrow and captivity and see the condition they were brought into. Calvin calls this the climax of their miseries and explains why a word should count worse than a wound: they should be so far from receiving consolation that on every side their misery would meet with taunts, and nothing more bitterly wounds the wretched than to be harassed by reproaches. He finds an antithesis implied besides, between the ignominy God now assigns them and the extraordinary dignity with which he had honoured them.

Ellicott marks it as the exact contrary of the promise that all the people of the earth should see the name of the Lord named upon them and be afraid, and observes that it was verified in the first captivity and did not wait for the last dispersion, the same threat having been repeated to Solomon and taken up by Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Keil and Delitzsch add the mechanism, that the nation would be thrust into bondage among a people it did not know and become a proverb to all nations whither God should drive it, treating the three words as one rising figure rather than three penalties.

themes: a byword as a distinct stroke
reproach worse than wounds
the promise turned inside out
verified before the last dispersion

38.pericope_label: Seed, vine, olive, and children lost

schools.summary: Gill fixes the reference before anything else, that these verses concern Israel while still in their own land, before the captivity, and not their present circumstances. Calvin reads the sequence as a set of different causes for one scarcity — the locust consuming the seed, worms devouring the bunches, olives withering and falling of themselves — by which God admonishes them that he has innumerable ministers at hand to destroy the transgressors by famine. Whenever we see insects attacking the fruits, he says, we should remember that God is putting forth his arm to take away the food he had given; philosophers can discover why more are generated in one year than another, but Moses teaches that they never trouble us except by God's command.

Keil and Delitzsch keep to the words: the olive is not merely barren, since the verb means it would be rooted out or plundered, and they argue the form against the parsing that would make it drop its fruit of itself. The creature named at the end they call the buzzer, from a root meaning to buzz, a rhetorical epithet for the locust rather than the grasshopper, since a grasshopper does not injure enough for the strong verb used here. They look ahead to the stranger rising very high, rejecting the explanation that he prospered because he had no landed possession, and holding instead that he and all his goods would be exempted from the curse, as Israel had been exempted from the plagues of Egypt.

themes: much seed and little harvest
the buzzer, not the grasshopper
insects as ministers of vengeance
why the stranger is exempt

43.pericope_label: The stranger above, and Israel below

schools.summary: Gill spells out the rising — above them in wealth, power, honour and dignity, so that one who had been a proselyte of the gate should stand vastly above them — and reports Manasseh Ben Israel referring the words to the Samaritans, though he takes the design to be simply how abject Israel should become abroad; on the lending he is careful that the point is the change of condition and not the kindness of either party. Calvin reads the debt itself as the proof, since those in debt are under the power of their creditors and Solomon's saying is found true; the Israelites must have felt God against them when they became suppliants to their own guests. He enters his usual caution, that poverty as well as wealth is in God's hands, and that God often chastises his own children with want without ceasing to be their Father, while bestowing abundance on the reprobate for their destruction.
Wesley catches the reversal in a phrase: the stranger within thy gates, who formerly honoured and served thee, and some of whom were glad of the crumbs that fell from thy table.

Keil and Delitzsch give the same reading in a sentence, that what happens here is the exact opposite of the two promises earlier in the chapter; and they mark where the address is going, since at the next pause it returns to its own beginning, with the curses for a sign and a wonder upon the seed for ever — the for ever restricted to the generation smitten, without involving the perpetual rejection of the nation or the impossibility of a holy seed.

themes: glad of the crumbs from thy table
the borrower servant to the lender
poverty and wealth both in God’s hands
how far the for ever reaches

schools.summary: Gill only gathers the reference, that all these curses means those already related as well as those that follow. Calvin reads the verse as closing every exit: it takes away all hope of alleviation, since God's scourges shall not cease until the people have repented, the word pursue removing all hope of escape and overtake laying hold of them tenaciously. The sum is that the ungodly by their subterfuges only accumulate heavier punishments on themselves. Why they should be a sign and a wonder he explains from the effect on the onlooker, since those little moved by God's common judgments are compelled to attend to prodigies; and he notices what is reproved besides their contempt of the law — their ingratitude, that they served not God with joyfulness when he had been so generous.

Henry traces the history: plucked from off the land not only by the Babylonish captivity and the Roman destruction but afterwards, when they were forbidden to set foot in the city; no rest of body and none of mind, banished from country to country, recalled and banished again. It is amazing, he says, that a people so long the favourites of heaven should be so cast off, and yet that a people scattered among all nations should be kept distinct. He draws two conclusions — that the accomplishment of the predictions shows Moses spoke by the Spirit of God, and that we should learn to stand in awe and not to sin — and closes where the chapter cannot, by turning to the remedy, that Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law by being made a curse for us.

Wesley thinks Moses has been foretelling the Babylonish captivity until now, and that from here he foretells the last destruction by the Romans; the present state of the Jewish nation answers the prediction so exactly that it is an incontestable proof of the divine authority of the Scriptures.

Ellicott qualifies the last word: destroyed does not mean exterminated, the root being connected with smiting and the idea rather to crush. Keil and Delitzsch describe the motive behind the passage, that love to his people and the desire to preserve them from the curse impel the faithful servant of the Lord to depict its horrors more minutely still.

themes: pursued, overtaken, and not exterminated
punishments that awaken astonishment
kept distinct though scattered
redeemed from the curse of the law

46.pericope_label: A sign and a wonder, and the service exchanged

schools.summary: Gill turns the sign and the wonder into an argument: the curses were to remain visible, so as to be observed as a sign of God's displeasure and of the truth of divine revelation, and what he finds the greater wonder is the survival — that a people so calamitously used should still continue a distinct people, a standing miracle he thinks sufficient to convince the most hardened deist. He puts the failure plainly, that they did not serve the Lord by attending his worship and keeping his commandments, and therefore should serve other lords.

Clarke says it in a sentence: because they would not serve God, they became slaves to men. Wesley presses the same paradox from the other side, that it is amazing a people so incorporated should be so universally dispersed, and that a people scattered among all nations should mix with none of them but, like Cain, be fugitives and vagabonds and yet so marked as to be known.

Keil and Delitzsch put the weight on the two adverbial clauses: it was because Israel had not served the Lord with joy and gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things, that it would serve its enemies in hunger and thirst and nakedness and wear an iron yoke. The contrast, on their reading, is not merely between serving God and serving men, but between serving in plenty with a glad heart and serving in destitution under a yoke.

themes: a standing miracle to the deist
scattered yet unmixed
because they would not serve God
plenty with gladness against want under a yoke

schools.summary: Gill grants that Babylon is called a nation from far but denies it was ever from the end of the earth, and argues for Rome, whose emperors and armies were fetched from Britain, once reckoned the end of the earth; he cites Manasseh Ben Israel for the same view and for the soldiers Vespasian drew from England, France and Spain. Calvin holds out for the Chaldeans and reads the strange language as the cruellest detail, since where there can be no oral communication there is no room for entreaties, which sometimes awaken even the savage to mercy; the prophets, he observes, took their very form of expression from Moses, lest the Jews should proudly despise threats interwoven with the law.

Clarke agrees with Gill and adds two proofs: the eagle was the very animal borne on all the Roman standards, and the tongue not understood is the Latin, than which no language was more foreign to the idiom of the Hebrew.

Ellicott sets Jeremiah's mighty and ancient nation beside the verse and grants only that the eagles of Rome may be alluded to, since of the Chaldeans too it is said they shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat. On the unintelligible tongue he adds an observation of his own day, from a learned Jewish friend, that hundreds of the dispersed never attain the least acquaintance with the language of the countries they live in — not from lack of ability but from a paralysis of the understanding outside a certain range of thought. Keil and Delitzsch describe what such a foe leaves, consuming everything gained by agriculture and stock-breeding until the fenced walls Israel trusted in came down.

debates: Which nation is meant. Gill and Clarke argue for Rome, from the phrase 'the end of the earth', the Roman eagle and the Latin tongue; Calvin and Ellicott hold out for the Chaldeans, on the ground that Jeremiah quotes these very words of them.
themes: Rome or the Chaldeans
the eagle on the standards
a tongue that leaves no room for pleading
strong of face and pitiless

52.pericope_label: The siege, and what it drives them to

schools.summary: Gill takes the gates for their cities and walled towns and will not describe what the siege drives them to beyond saying that nothing can be more shocking and unnatural. Calvin reads the verse as the demolition of a false confidence, since the number of their towns had inspired them with courage and their trust in high walls is equally vain, whether the fortresses are thrown down by engines or surrender from the mere length of the siege; the repetition magnifies the evil, that they should be pressed so sorely in the land God had given them. Of the eating he explains why it is the worst of the portents: it is an act more than tragical that parents should eat the offspring whose love is so naturally implanted that many have died to secure their children's safety — and the brutality is heightened by the persons, men accustomed to delicacies refusing a share even of that food to their wives.

Clarke names the besiegers and the manner, Nebuchadnezzar first and Titus afterwards, casting lines of circumvallation as our Lord predicted, and reads in all thy gates as showing that the subjugation would be complete.

Ellicott supplies an instance from each side of the history — Jeremiah's last two fenced cities still besieged, and the capture of Jotapata recorded specially by Josephus — and points to where the eating was fulfilled, in the siege of Samaria and in Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar. Keil and Delitzsch mark it as the refrain of what follows, the words about the siege and the straitness returning with their appalling sound.

themes: a confidence in walls demolished
lines of circumvallation
the refrain of siege and straitness
the pitiful women maddened by hunger

schools.summary: Gill points out that the man instanced is not the rustic used to hard living but one bred tenderly who had fared sumptuously, and the woman because her sex is the more pitiful and compassionate; he takes the young one for the secundine, following the Targum of Jonathan and Aben Ezra, so that the delicate woman should eat the membrane and then the child wrapped in it, though Jarchi understands it of little children.

Clarke sees a species of tautology in the two clauses and removes it by rendering the word literally as her secondines, as the Septuagint and Luther did; so read, it marks the deepest distress, the mother regretting that her child was brought forth into such suffering. He reports Kennicott's emendation besides, a change of one word making the clause read she shall boil that which cometh out from between her feet, which would match the prophecy to the two women of Samaria — but sees no absolute need of it, and says the whole was literally fulfilled in the woman who boiled and ate her own child at the Roman siege. Wesley glosses the evil eye as unkind and envious, covetous to monopolise these dainty bits and grudging that the dearest relations should have any part.

Ellicott names her Mary of Beth-ezob and points to the story told with horrible minuteness by Josephus and again by Eusebius, adding that the secrecy of the deed was one of its horrors — which is the very thing the verse specifies; he sums the structure as a complication of horrors, in which they eat some of their children and then refuse to share even that food. Keil and Delitzsch describe the delicacy from the Hebrew, the woman who had never set her foot to the ground, being always carried on a litter or an ass, and mark the turn that comes next, that these calamities are still not the end.

outliers: Kennicott's proposed emendation, reported by Clarke, which would change one word so that the verse reads 'she shall boil' and align it exactly with the siege of Samaria.
themes: the delicate rather than the hardened
her secondines or her children
Mary of Beth-ezob
the secrecy as part of the horror

schools.summary: Gill identifies the book as Deuteronomy, in which the laws before delivered are repeated and some new ones added. Calvin fastens on the phrase observe to do and on its severity: even believers are impeded by the infirmity of the flesh, so what is demanded is sedulous and diligent heed, and it is a harsh threat that leaves transgression without remission — but Moses was thus severe so that the people, convinced of their condemnation, should betake themselves to God's mercy, since no one longs after Christ until he abandons all confidence in his works. The clause about fearing the name he takes for the fountain-head of the whole, since all virtues are but smoke that do not spring from the fear of God. On the word wonderful he rejects the constructions that make it separate or increase, preferring extraordinary modes of vengeance surpassing human comprehension, and reads the second epithet as continued duration rather than certainty. The diseases of Egypt, he adds, are not those Israel suffered but those they had watched the Egyptians labouring under.

Ellicott sets promise and threat side by side: against the word that if they hearkened God would put none of the diseases of Egypt upon them, for he is Jehovah that healeth thee, stands the word that they shall know he is Jehovah that smiteth — the healer and the smiter being one. Keil and Delitzsch render the strokes as extraordinary and lasting, note that the verb means to turn back since Israel had been freed from those diseases at the exodus, and distinguish the diseases written in the law from the strokes that are the rest of the plagues.

themes: observe to do, and perfect obedience
the fear of God as the root of virtue
wonderful, or extraordinary and lasting
Jehovah that healeth and that smiteth

61.pericope_label: Every plague not written, and the few left

schools.summary: Gill reads the open clause as leaving nothing out, whatever sickness could be named or was at any time among men, and supplies the histories of the reduction — very few left in Judea when Jerusalem was taken, and Josephus' reckoning of eleven hundred thousand slain and ninety-seven thousand made prisoners. Calvin finds here a confirmation of his earlier point that the sickness is the particular and the plague the wider term, and draws out the force of the addition, that after so many punishments God declares he is armed with yet other weapons; and he will not let the comparison with the stars be read as rhetoric, since it had been promised to Abraham that his seed should be so numerous, so that their reduction to a handful was a signal token of wrath.

Wesley presses the hard half rather than softening it: God's indignation will be so great that it will be a pleasure to him to take vengeance, for though he does not delight in the death of a sinner in itself, he delights in glorifying his justice upon incorrigible sinners.

Ellicott needs only the apostle's words, that it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Keil and Delitzsch call the sentence about God's pleasure the hardest in the chapter, and explain the bold anthropomorphism as Moses removing the nation's last prop of false confidence in the mercy of God, since the holiness of his love demands the punishment of those who despise the riches of his goodness, so that he displays his glory in judgment no less than in blessing.

themes: every plague not written in the book
the stars of heaven reduced to a handful
God rejoicing to destroy
the last prop of false confidence

schools.summary: Gill notes their present dispersion and lists the machinery of the unrest — cruel edicts, heavy fines, exorbitant taxes, the searches of the courts of inquisition — observing that the Jews themselves own the passage fulfilled in them. Calvin reads these verses as a descent by steps: banishment first, which was more painful to Israel than to others since Canaan had been promised them; then a scattering, since exile all together in one corner would have been more tolerable for the very association; then the want of rest, the most wretched state of all, to serve tyrannical conquerors and have no certain master. He enlarges the resulting fear deliberately, because the fear of spiritual punishment affects ungodly men so little, and illustrates it from Dionysius' sword hung by a thread over the flatterer who had called him happy: tranquillity of mind can only arise from having God as our keeper.

Clarke says how literally the scattering has been fulfilled, and reads the two clauses as insecurity under every government and an ever-disappointed expectation of the Messiah. Wesley has them tossed from place to place and sold from person to person, or wandering like Cain.

Ellicott is careful about the idolatry, since we do not know of Israel falling into actual idol-worship in dispersion except in Egypt and possibly Babylon, though they were slaves to the worshippers of other gods; he calls the persecutions among the most fearful phenomena of history and glosses the failing eyes from Rashi as looking for salvation and it cometh not. Keil and Delitzsch put the homelessness plainly, no place where Israel could set its foot down and have peace in its heart.

themes: banishment, scattering, and no rest
the sword of Dionysius
slaves to idolaters, if not idolaters
looking for salvation, and it cometh not

66.pericope_label: Thy life shall hang in doubt

schools.summary: Gill keeps it outward and simple, the doubt being whether the enemy will spare the life or not, and imagines the man wishing he may get through the day well, fearing his life will be taken before night.

Wesley allows either cause: that they are in the hands of enemies who have the power and want no will to destroy them, or that the terrors of their own mind and the guilt of conscience make them fear even where no fear is.

Keil and Delitzsch give the figure exactly — the life hanging by a thin thread before the eyes, which any moment might tear down — and set beside it Luther's remark that he had never seen a passage describing more clearly the misery of a guilty conscience, since this is just how a man is affected who knows that God is offended. On the morning and the evening they put both halves together, the wish at each hour that it were the other, from a perpetual dread of what the day or the night would bring. Ellicott quotes Rashi for the thought as the man himself would frame it: perhaps I shall die to-day by the sword that cometh upon me.

themes: a life hung by a thread
Luther on the guilty conscience
would God it were even
dread of whatever the hour holds

schools.summary: Gill will not refer the verse to the flight into Egypt after Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, that being against God's express command, and takes what is chiefly meant to be their case under the Romans, when Titus sent all above seventeen to the works in Egypt. Calvin makes the same distinction as Keil about the road: it was most to be desired that they should never be carried back into that wilderness, and to bring them back was in a manner to blot out the grace of redemption; if any object that a people could not be conveyed in ships through dry places, the reply is easy, since captivity is what is spoken of.

Clarke takes the verb as exposing oneself for sale, the people being vagrants who wished to be slaves for the sake of necessaries, and no man would buy, since even the Romans thought it a reproach to have a Jew for a slave. He closes the chapter rather than the verse, calling it astonishing, containing prophecies delivered three thousand years ago and now fulfilling, and adds that in the most correct Hebrew Bibles the first verse of the next chapter is counted as the last of this one. Wesley reads the way as the end of the journey rather than the road, and finds the sting in the reminder that they once went over the sea without ships, God drying it up before them; he ends with a story of a man who tore the leaf out of his Bible in rage at these threatenings — but to what purpose deface a copy while the original remains unchangeable.

Keil and Delitzsch state why this is kept for last, that Moses mentions the worst, since if the exodus was the birth of the nation of God its return would be its death; in ships means in a way that cut off escape, and the clause about the way is not an explanation of the ships but a strengthening of the threat. Ellicott reports Rashi's reading of the last clause but prefers the word as Nehemiah uses it of brethren redeemed from the heathen: they shall be sold to their enemies and none will redeem them.

themes: the return that would be the nation’s death
in ships, and by a road never to be seen again
offered for sale and refused
the leaf torn out of the Bible
